nodes.title: EC2 Auto Scaling groups and capacity

prompts.label: WHAT ARE EC2 AUTO SCALING GROUPS AND CAPACITY SETTINGS?
prompts.placeholder: An EC2 Auto Scaling group (ASG) maintains a fleet of EC2 instances from a launch…

reveal.text: An EC2 Auto Scaling group (ASG) maintains a fleet of EC2 instances from a launch template and works toward a desired capacity within configured minimum and maximum bounds.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?
prompts.placeholder: Use an ASG when instance capacity should recover from failures or change with demand.

reveal.text: Use an ASG when instance capacity should recover from failures or change with demand.

prompts.label: CONCRETE EXAMPLE
prompts.placeholder: An Auto Scaling group has `Min=2`, `Desired=4`, and `Max=10`.

reveal.text: An Auto Scaling group has `Min=2`, `Desired=4`, and `Max=10`. A scaling policy requests 12 instances during a spike, but the group stops at 10 because `MaxSize` is the hard upper bound.

prompts.label: EXAM / SCENARIO CLUE
prompts.placeholder: If scaling stops unexpectedly, verify maximum capacity and launch-template/instance-launch errors.

reveal.text: If scaling stops unexpectedly, verify maximum capacity and launch-template/instance-launch errors.

prompts.label: ASG CAPACITY BOUNDS
prompts.placeholder: Compare: Minimum • Desired • Maximum

cells.meaning: Lowest capacity the ASG should maintain.
cells.failure: Unexpected scale-in stops at this floor.
ASG works back toward this number.
Scale-out stops even while demand remains high.

prompts.label: READ THE REAL CONFIG
prompts.placeholder: Key lines: Minimum capacity • Desired capacity • Maximum capacity • Launch template

reveal.code:
Resources:
  WebAsg:
    Type: AWS::AutoScaling::AutoScalingGroup
    Properties:
      MinSize: '2'
      DesiredCapacity: '4'
      MaxSize: '10'
      LaunchTemplate:
        LaunchTemplateId: lt-0123456789abcdef0
        Version: '3'

reveal.text: A scaling policy tells Auto Scaling when and how to change capacity.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?

reveal.text: Choose target tracking for continuous metric targets, step scaling for different reactions to alarm severity, scheduled scaling for known time-based demand, and predictive scaling for forecastable recurring demand.

nodes.title: Instance warmup and health-check grace period

prompts.label: WHAT ARE INSTANCE WARMUP AND THE HEALTH-CHECK GRACE PERIOD?
prompts.placeholder: Instance warmup controls when a new instance fully contributes to scaling decisions. Health-check grace period…

reveal.text: Instance warmup keeps newly launched capacity from affecting dynamic scaling decisions too soon. The health-check grace period gives a new InService instance time to initialize before Auto Scaling replaces it because of configured health-check failures.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?
prompts.placeholder: Tune them to real startup behavior. Very short values can cause scaling churn or premature…

reveal.text: Tune them to real startup behavior. Very short values can cause scaling churn or premature replacement.

prompts.label: CONCRETE EXAMPLE
prompts.placeholder: A new instance needs 4 minutes to start the application, but Auto Scaling begins acting on health failures after 1 minute and replaces it.

reveal.text: A new instance needs 4 minutes before its application is ready. The load balancer reports it unhealthy after 1 minute, and Auto Scaling replaces it too early. Increase the health-check grace period to match real startup behavior. Instance warmup solves a different scaling-stabilization problem.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: Warmup • Health-check grace

cells.use: Avoids reacting too soon to fresh capacity
Avoids terminating instances before the app is ready

prompts.label: EXAM / SCENARIO CLUE
prompts.placeholder: New instances are replaced before startup completes -> health-check grace is a primary clue.

reveal.text: New instances are replaced before startup completes -> health-check grace is a primary clue.

prompts.label: WHAT IS QUEUE-DRIVEN SCALING?
prompts.placeholder: Queue-driven scaling adjusts worker capacity based on outstanding work, often using backlog per worker rather…

reveal.text: Queue-driven scaling adjusts worker capacity based on outstanding work, often using backlog per worker rather than CPU alone.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?
prompts.placeholder: Use it when the amount of queued work better represents demand than host utilization.

reveal.text: Use it when the amount of queued work better represents demand than host utilization.

prompts.label: CONCRETE EXAMPLE
prompts.placeholder: An SQS queue has 12,000 visible messages and 20 workers, so backlog is about 600 messages per worker.

reveal.text: An SQS queue has 12,000 visible messages and 20 workers, so backlog is about 600 messages per worker. CPU is only 25%. Scaling on backlog per worker can represent demand better than CPU for this workload.

prompts.label: EXAM / SCENARIO CLUE
prompts.placeholder: Workers have low CPU but the queue keeps growing -> scale on backlog or backlog…

reveal.text: Workers have low CPU but the queue keeps growing -> scale on backlog or backlog per instance.

prompts.label: SQS QUEUE CHOICES
prompts.placeholder: Compare Standard, FIFO, and dead-letter queue behavior.

cells.behavior: At-least-once delivery; best-effort ordering; very high throughput
cells.use: Order is not strict and consumers are idempotent

cells.behavior: Preserves message-group ordering and supports deduplication/exactly-once processing semantics within SQS constraints
Receives messages that fail processing repeatedly after the configured receive threshold

prompts.label: WHAT ARE CLOUDFRONT CACHING POLICIES?
prompts.placeholder: CloudFront caches content at edge locations. The cache key decides which request attributes create separate…

reveal.text: CloudFront caches content at edge locations. The cache key decides which request attributes create separate cached objects; origin request policy controls additional values sent to the origin without necessarily varying the cache.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?
prompts.placeholder: Keep the cache key as small as correctness allows. Unnecessary headers, cookies, or query strings…

reveal.text: Keep the cache key as small as correctness allows. Unnecessary headers, cookies, or query strings reduce cache-hit ratio.

prompts.label: CONCRETE EXAMPLE
prompts.placeholder: Requests `/logo.png?tracking_user=123` and `/logo.png?tracking_user=456` return identical content.

reveal.text: Requests `/logo.png?tracking_user=123` and `/logo.png?tracking_user=456` return identical content. If that tracking parameter is included in the cache key, CloudFront stores separate variants and hit ratio drops for no benefit.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: Cache policy • Origin request policy

cells.what: Controls cache key and TTL-related behavior
Controls additional request values forwarded to origin
cells.use: Can forward values without putting all of them in the cache key

prompts.label: EXAM / SCENARIO CLUE
prompts.placeholder: Low cache-hit ratio caused by tracking query parameters -> remove irrelevant values from the cache…

reveal.text: Low cache-hit ratio caused by tracking query parameters -> remove irrelevant values from the cache key.

prompts.label: HOW DO ELASTICACHE FOR VALKEY/REDIS OSS AND MEMCACHED DIFFER?
prompts.placeholder: Amazon ElastiCache is a managed in-memory caching service. Valkey/Redis OSS and Memcached have different data…

reveal.text: Amazon ElastiCache is a managed in-memory caching service. Valkey/Redis OSS and Memcached have different data models and availability features.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?
prompts.placeholder: Choose Valkey/Redis OSS for richer data structures, replication, and Multi-AZ patterns; choose Memcached for a…

reveal.text: Choose Valkey/Redis OSS for richer data structures, replication, and Multi-AZ patterns; choose Memcached for a simpler distributed cache where those Redis-style features are not needed.

prompts.label: CONCRETE EXAMPLE
prompts.placeholder: A shopping-cart service needs replicated in-memory data and automatic failover, which fits Valkey/Redis OSS features better than Memcached.

reveal.text: A shopping-cart service needs replicated in-memory data and automatic failover, which fits Valkey/Redis OSS features better than Memcached. A disposable, simple distributed cache where replication semantics are unnecessary can fit Memcached.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: Valkey / Redis OSS • Memcached

cells.what: Rich data structures and replication options
cells.use: Supports HA patterns such as Multi-AZ
Scale-out cache without Redis-style replication model

prompts.label: EXAM / SCENARIO CLUE
prompts.placeholder: Need replication/failover or richer data structures -> Valkey/Redis OSS.

reveal.text: Need replication/failover or richer data structures -> Valkey/Redis OSS.

prompts.label: DAX VS ELASTICACHE
prompts.placeholder: Compare DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) with ElastiCache.

cells.fit: Microsecond caching for eventually consistent DynamoDB reads with a DynamoDB-compatible API
cells.clue: DynamoDB is the source and read latency must drop to microseconds

cells.fit: General-purpose application/database caching, sessions, rich Redis/Valkey structures, or Memcached
cells.clue: Cache is not specifically a transparent DynamoDB read accelerator

prompts.label: HOW DO RDS AND AURORA SCALE?
prompts.placeholder: Managed database scaling can change compute, storage, or read capacity depending on which resource is…

reveal.text: Managed database scaling can change compute, storage, or read capacity depending on which resource is constrained.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?
prompts.placeholder: Scale the layer that is actually under pressure: DB instance class for compute/memory, storage autoscaling…

reveal.text: Scale the layer that is actually under pressure: DB instance class for compute/memory, storage autoscaling for allocated storage growth, and read replicas/Aurora replica scaling for read demand.

prompts.label: CONCRETE EXAMPLE
prompts.placeholder: A database has `CPUUtilization Avg=28%` and plenty of read capacity, but free storage is falling toward zero.

reveal.text: A database has `CPUUtilization Avg=28%` and plenty of read capacity, but free storage is falling toward zero. Storage autoscaling addresses storage growth. Adding a read replica would solve the wrong problem.

prompts.label: EXAM / SCENARIO CLUE
prompts.placeholder: Do not solve a storage-capacity problem by adding read replicas, or a read-scaling problem by…

reveal.text: Do not solve a storage-capacity problem by adding read replicas, or a read-scaling problem by only increasing storage.

prompts.label: AURORA SERVERLESS V2
prompts.placeholder: Aurora Serverless v2 scales database compute in Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) inside a configured range as demand changes.

reveal.text: Use Aurora Serverless v2 when an Aurora workload needs fine-grained automatic database compute scaling instead of manually sizing fixed DB instances. Each serverless writer or reader has capacity measured in ACUs and scales within configured minimum and maximum capacity settings.

prompts.label: WHAT ARE DYNAMODB CAPACITY MODES?
prompts.placeholder: DynamoDB offers on-demand capacity, where AWS handles request capacity automatically, and provisioned capacity, where read/write…

reveal.text: DynamoDB offers on-demand capacity, where AWS handles request capacity automatically, and provisioned capacity, where read/write capacity is configured and can use auto scaling.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?
prompts.placeholder: Use on-demand for unpredictable/spiky workloads or operational simplicity; use provisioned with auto scaling when planned…

reveal.text: Use on-demand for unpredictable/spiky workloads or operational simplicity; use provisioned with auto scaling when planned capacity and utilization management fit the workload.

prompts.label: CONCRETE EXAMPLE
prompts.placeholder: A new ticket-sale workload can jump from almost no traffic to thousands of requests per second without a predictable schedule.

reveal.text: A new ticket-sale workload can jump from almost no traffic to thousands of requests per second without a predictable schedule. On-demand capacity reduces planning. A stable workload with known throughput can justify provisioned capacity with auto scaling.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: On-demand • Provisioned

cells.what: Configured RCU/WCU with optional auto scaling

prompts.label: EXAM / SCENARIO CLUE
prompts.placeholder: Unknown or highly variable traffic with minimal capacity planning -> on-demand.

reveal.text: Unknown or highly variable traffic with minimal capacity planning -> on-demand.

prompts.label: WHAT ARE ALB, NLB, AND GWLB?
prompts.placeholder: Elastic Load Balancing distributes traffic to healthy targets. ALB, NLB, and GWLB serve different network…

reveal.text: Elastic Load Balancing normally distributes traffic to healthy targets. ALB, NLB, and GWLB serve different network layers and use cases. ALB and NLB also have documented fail-open behavior when healthy targets are unavailable.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?
prompts.placeholder: Choose ALB for HTTP/HTTPS Layer 7 routing, NLB for high-performance Layer 4 TCP/UDP/TLS, and GWLB…

reveal.text: Choose ALB for HTTP/HTTPS Layer 7 routing, NLB for high-performance Layer 4 TCP/UDP/TLS, and GWLB for inserting and scaling virtual network appliances.

prompts.label: CONCRETE EXAMPLE
prompts.placeholder: An HTTP API must route `/images/*` to one target group and `/api/*` to another, which points to ALB Layer-7 routing.

reveal.text: An HTTP API must route `/images/*` to one target group and `/api/*` to another, which points to ALB Layer-7 routing. A high-throughput TCP service on port 443 that does not need HTTP-aware routing is a different NLB-style requirement.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: ALB • NLB • GWLB

prompts.label: EXAM / SCENARIO CLUE
prompts.placeholder: Path-based HTTP routing -> ALB; TCP/UDP transport load balancing -> NLB.

reveal.text: Path-based HTTP routing -> ALB; TCP/UDP transport load balancing -> NLB.

nodes.title: Target groups, health checks, deregistration, and cross-zone

prompts.label: HOW DO TARGET HEALTH, DEREGISTRATION, AND CROSS-ZONE LOAD BALANCING WORK?
prompts.placeholder: A target group defines where a load balancer sends traffic and how target health is…

reveal.text: A target group defines where a load balancer sends traffic and how target health is checked. Deregistration delay lets in-flight work drain when a target is removed.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?
prompts.placeholder: Troubleshoot target eligibility from health checks first. Cross-zone behavior affects how load-balancer nodes distribute traffic…

reveal.text: Troubleshoot target eligibility from health checks first. Cross-zone load balancing controls whether a load-balancer node can use targets in other enabled Availability Zones. For ALB it is enabled at the load-balancer level; for NLB it is disabled by default at the load-balancer level.

prompts.label: CONCRETE EXAMPLE
prompts.placeholder: An ALB target is registered but shows `unhealthy` because `/health` returns HTTP 500.

reveal.text: An ALB target is registered but `/health` returns HTTP 500, so the target becomes unhealthy. While healthy alternatives remain, new requests normally stop going to that target. If all registered targets are unhealthy, ALB can fail open and route to unhealthy targets. Deregistration delay is different: it gives in-flight requests time to finish when a target is removed.

prompts.label: WHAT HEALTH DATA CAN LOOK LIKE
prompts.placeholder: ALB shows HealthyHostCount=0 while ECS tasks restart: inspect target-health reason and task/container logs.

cells.meaning: No target is currently considered healthy
The app health endpoint is failing
Application startup/readiness is likely the root cause

prompts.label: ELB HEALTH CHECK VS ROUTE 53 HEALTH CHECK
prompts.placeholder: ELB decides whether to send traffic to a target; Route 53 can make DNS routing/failover decisions.

cells.effect: Normally controls target eligibility; ALB can fail open if all targets are unhealthy

cells.scope: DNS endpoint/record health or supported alias target health
cells.effect: Which DNS answer is selected for policies such as failover
cells.example: Primary endpoint unhealthy → answer secondary failover record

prompts.label: EXAM / SCENARIO CLUE
prompts.placeholder: A target is registered but receives no traffic -> verify health-check status and target-group settings…

reveal.text: A target is registered but receives no traffic -> verify target health and target-group settings first. Remember the documented fail-open exception when no healthy targets remain.

prompts.label: HOW DO ROUTE 53 HEALTH CHECKS AND FAILOVER WORK?
prompts.placeholder: Route 53 can make DNS routing decisions using health checks or supported alias-target health through…

reveal.text: Route 53 can make DNS routing decisions using health checks or supported alias-target health through Evaluate Target Health.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?
prompts.placeholder: Use failover routing for active/passive DNS behavior when traffic should move from a primary endpoint…

reveal.text: Use failover routing for active/passive DNS behavior when traffic should move from a primary endpoint to a secondary endpoint based on health.

prompts.label: CONCRETE EXAMPLE
prompts.placeholder: The primary application endpoint in `us-east-1` fails its Route 53 health evaluation.

reveal.text: The primary application endpoint in `us-east-1` fails its Route 53 health evaluation. With failover records configured, DNS answers can shift to the secondary endpoint. DNS caching means clients may not all switch at exactly the same instant.

prompts.label: EXAM / SCENARIO CLUE
prompts.placeholder: DNS active/passive routing with a primary and secondary endpoint -> Route 53 failover.

reveal.text: DNS active/passive routing with a primary and secondary endpoint -> Route 53 failover.

prompts.label: READ THE REAL CONFIG
prompts.placeholder: Key lines: Primary record • Health evaluation • Secondary record

reveal.code:
Parameters:
  PrimaryHealthCheckId:
    Type: String
  SecondaryHealthCheckId:
    Type: String
Resources:
  PrimaryRecord:
    Type: AWS::Route53::RecordSet
    Properties:
      HostedZoneName: example.com.
      Name: app.example.com.
      Type: A
      TTL: '60'
      ResourceRecords:
        - 192.0.2.10
      SetIdentifier: primary
      Failover: PRIMARY
      HealthCheckId: !Ref PrimaryHealthCheckId
  SecondaryRecord:
    Type: AWS::Route53::RecordSet
    Properties:
      HostedZoneName: example.com.
      Name: app.example.com.
      Type: A
      TTL: '60'
      ResourceRecords:
        - 192.0.2.20
      SetIdentifier: secondary
      Failover: SECONDARY
      HealthCheckId: !Ref SecondaryHealthCheckId

prompts.label: HOW DO RDS MULTI-AZ AND READ REPLICAS DIFFER?
prompts.placeholder: RDS Multi-AZ is primarily an availability/failover design. Read replicas are primarily for read scaling and…

reveal.text: RDS has two Multi-AZ architectures. A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment uses one non-readable standby for failover. A Multi-AZ DB cluster has one writer and two readable standby instances across three Availability Zones. Read replicas are primarily asynchronous read-scaling copies.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?
prompts.placeholder: Choose based on the requirement: automatic managed HA failover points to Multi-AZ; additional read capacity…

reveal.text: Choose based on the requirement: automatic managed HA failover points to Multi-AZ; additional read capacity points to read replicas.

prompts.label: CONCRETE EXAMPLE
prompts.placeholder: The primary RDS instance fails.

reveal.text: The primary RDS instance fails. In a Multi-AZ design, AWS can fail over to a standby for availability. A read replica is primarily for read scaling; it should not be chosen just because the word 'replica' sounds highly available.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: Multi-AZ DB instance • Multi-AZ DB cluster • Read replica

cells.read_behavior: Standby does not serve read traffic
Two standby DB instances can also serve reads
Asynchronous copy used for reads; promotion is a separate action

prompts.label: EXAM / SCENARIO CLUE
prompts.placeholder: "Automatic failover" -> Multi-AZ. "Scale read traffic" -> read replica.

reveal.text: "Automatic failover" -> Multi-AZ. "Scale read traffic" -> read replica.

prompts.label: WHAT IS A HIGHLY AVAILABLE WEB TIER?
prompts.placeholder: A highly available web tier spreads entry points, load balancing, compute capacity, and data services…

reveal.text: A highly available web tier spreads entry points, load balancing, compute capacity, and data services across independent failure zones where possible.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?
prompts.placeholder: Design by failure layer: Route 53 or resilient endpoint, multi-AZ load balancing, Auto Scaling across…

reveal.text: Design by failure layer: Route 53 or resilient endpoint, multi-AZ load balancing, Auto Scaling across AZs, and an HA data tier.

prompts.label: CONCRETE EXAMPLE
prompts.placeholder: A resilient web app uses Route 53, an ALB across multiple AZs, an Auto Scaling group spanning those AZs, and an HA database tier.

reveal.text: A resilient web app uses Route 53, an ALB across multiple AZs, an Auto Scaling group spanning those AZs, and an HA database tier. If one AZ fails, healthy capacity remains in another AZ instead of the whole request path disappearing.

prompts.label: EXAM / SCENARIO CLUE
prompts.placeholder: Avoid a single-AZ dependency anywhere in the request path when the requirement is AZ fault…

reveal.text: Avoid a single-AZ dependency anywhere in the request path when the requirement is AZ fault tolerance.

prompts.label: HOW IT FLOWS
prompts.placeholder: Flow: DNS / entry point → … → Highly available data tier

prompts.label: APPLICATION RECOVERY CONTROLLER: ZONAL SHIFT
prompts.placeholder: An Availability Zone is impaired but the Region is healthy → ARC zonal shift can move supported resource traffic away from that AZ.

reveal.text: Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) includes zonal shift for supported resources. During a zonal impairment, a zonal shift can move traffic away from the affected Availability Zone. This differs from Route 53 regional DNS failover, which works at another routing layer.

nodes.title: AWS Backup plans, vaults, copies, and restore testing

prompts.label: WHAT ARE AWS BACKUP PLANS, VAULTS, COPIES, AND RESTORE TESTING?
prompts.placeholder: AWS Backup centrally manages supported backup policies, schedules, lifecycle/retention, vault storage, and copy operations.

reveal.text: AWS Backup centrally manages supported backup policies, schedules, lifecycle/retention, vault storage, and copy operations.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?
prompts.placeholder: Use backup copies for supported cross-Region/cross-account resilience and restore testing to verify that recovery points…

reveal.text: Use supported backup copies for cross-Region or cross-account resilience. Use restore testing to run scheduled restore jobs and measure whether recovery points can be restored. Optional validation can then check whether the restored workload actually works.

prompts.label: CONCRETE EXAMPLE
prompts.placeholder: A backup plan runs daily at 05:00, retains recovery points for 35 days, and copies supported backups to another Region.

reveal.text: A backup plan runs daily at 05:00, retains recovery points for 35 days, and copies supported backups to another Region. Monthly restore testing starts real restore jobs from selected recovery points and records completion and duration. An optional validation workflow can then check the restored workload.

prompts.label: EXAM / SCENARIO CLUE
prompts.placeholder: A compliant backup is not enough if it has never been restored; restore testing validates…

reveal.text: Restore testing verifies that scheduled restore jobs can complete from selected recovery points. Use optional restore-test validation when the requirement is to verify application or workload health after restore.

prompts.label: AWS BACKUP PARTS
prompts.placeholder: Compare: Backup plan • Backup vault • Copy action • Restore testing

cells.meaning: Schedule, windows, lifecycle, retention, copy rules.
Copies supported backups to another vault/Region/account.

cells.why: Proves recoverability, not just backup success.

prompts.label: READ THE REAL CONFIG
prompts.placeholder: Key lines: Backup plan • Backup vault • Schedule • Lifecycle / retention

reveal.code:
Resources:
  DailyBackupPlan:
    Type: AWS::Backup::BackupPlan
    Properties:
      BackupPlan:
        BackupPlanName: daily-prod
        BackupPlanRule:
          - RuleName: daily
            TargetBackupVault: prod-vault
            ScheduleExpression: cron(0 5 * * ? *)
            Lifecycle:
              DeleteAfterDays: 35

prompts.label: HOW DO EBS SNAPSHOTS AND AMIS DIFFER?
prompts.placeholder: An EBS snapshot is a point-in-time backup of EBS volume data. An Amazon Machine Image…

reveal.text: An EBS snapshot is a point-in-time backup of EBS volume data. An Amazon Machine Image (AMI) is a launchable EC2 image definition that references block-device snapshots plus image metadata.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?
prompts.placeholder: Use snapshots for volume backup/restore and AMIs for repeatable instance launch/replacement.

reveal.text: Use snapshots for volume backup/restore and AMIs for repeatable instance launch/replacement.

prompts.label: CONCRETE EXAMPLE
prompts.placeholder: A data volume is accidentally deleted: restore from an EBS snapshot.

reveal.text: A data volume is accidentally deleted: restore from an EBS snapshot. A fleet needs to launch new EC2 instances with a known OS/application image: use an AMI. The snapshot is volume backup data; the AMI is a launchable machine-image definition.

prompts.label: DON'T CONFUSE THESE
prompts.placeholder: Compare: EBS snapshot • AMI

cells.what: Launch EC2 instances with an image definition

prompts.label: EXAM / SCENARIO CLUE
prompts.placeholder: Need to create replacement EC2 instances from a known image -> AMI.

reveal.text: Need to create replacement EC2 instances from a known image -> AMI.

prompts.label: WHAT IS DATABASE POINT-IN-TIME RECOVERY?
prompts.placeholder: Point-in-time recovery (PITR) restores a database or table to a selected time within the available…

reveal.text: Point-in-time recovery (PITR) restores data to a selected time within the available recovery window. For Amazon RDS and DynamoDB, the restore creates a new DB instance or table instead of rewinding the source resource in place.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?
prompts.placeholder: Use it for accidental changes or corruption when the recovery point must be more precise…

reveal.text: Use it for accidental changes or corruption when the recovery point must be more precise than the latest manual snapshot.

prompts.label: CONCRETE EXAMPLE
prompts.placeholder: At 10:17 a user deletes rows accidentally.

reveal.text: At 10:17 a user deletes rows accidentally. PITR is enabled, so the team restores the database to 10:16 into a new restored resource, validates the data, and then performs the application recovery steps.

prompts.label: EXAM / SCENARIO CLUE
prompts.placeholder: Recover to the state just before an accidental deletion -> PITR.

reveal.text: Recover to the state just before an accidental deletion -> PITR.

nodes.title: S3 replication and FSx recovery features

prompts.label: WHAT ARE S3 REPLICATION AND FSX RECOVERY FEATURES?
prompts.placeholder: Storage recovery can use versioning, replication, backups, snapshots, or file-system-specific recovery features depending on the…

reveal.text: Storage recovery can use versioning, replication, backups, snapshots, or file-system-specific recovery features depending on the service.

prompts.label: WHEN DOES IT MATTER?
prompts.placeholder: S3 versioning protects object versions; replication can maintain copies under configured rules. FSx families provide…

reveal.text: S3 Versioning keeps multiple versions of an object so older data can be recovered. S3 replication copies eligible objects under configured rules and requires versioning on both the source and destination buckets. glossary.definition: A reusable EC2 launch configuration that defines settings such as the AMI, instance type, security groups, and other launch options.
An Auto Scaling feature that gradually replaces instances so a group can roll out a new launch template or configuration.
A pause point during instance launch or termination that gives your automation time to run before Auto Scaling continues.
A pool of pre-initialized EC2 instances that can enter an Auto Scaling group faster than launching completely from scratch.
Work waiting to be processed, such as messages still waiting in an SQS queue.
Safe to process more than once without changing the final result again. This helps applications handle duplicate messages.
First in, first out. In SQS FIFO queues, messages in the same message group are processed in order.
Dead-letter queue. It holds messages that repeatedly fail processing so they can be inspected or handled separately.
The request values CloudFront uses to decide whether two requests can use the same cached object.
The backend source CloudFront fetches content from when needed, such as an S3 bucket or a load balancer.
Time to live. It controls how long cached data or a DNS answer can be reused before it should be refreshed.
The share of requests served from cache instead of going back to the origin. A higher ratio usually means less origin work.
One partition of a larger dataset and workload. In clustered Valkey or Redis OSS, adding shards can spread data and traffic.
DynamoDB Accelerator. It is a managed in-memory cache designed to speed up DynamoDB reads.
Aurora Capacity Unit. Aurora Serverless v2 uses ACUs to measure and scale database compute and memory capacity.
Read Capacity Unit. In DynamoDB provisioned mode, RCUs represent configured read throughput capacity.
Write Capacity Unit. In DynamoDB provisioned mode, WCUs represent configured write throughput capacity.
The transport layer. Load balancing here works with protocols such as TCP and UDP instead of HTTP request details.
The application layer. For HTTP and HTTPS, a load balancer can use details such as host names and URL paths.
A load balancer component that waits for client connections on a configured protocol and port, then applies routing rules.
A load-balancer behavior where traffic can still be sent to unhealthy targets when no healthy targets remain.
Domain Name System. It translates names such as app.example.com into addresses or service endpoints clients can use.
Replication where a write is coordinated with another copy before the operation is considered complete.
Replication where the primary copy can accept a write before the secondary copy has fully caught up.
A saved state of a resource that can be used for a restore, such as a backup or snapshot.
How long a backup, recovery point, or other stored data is kept before it can expire or be deleted.
In a versioning-enabled S3 bucket, a simple delete can create a marker that hides older versions instead of erasing them immediately.
The normal ongoing cost of keeping a system ready before any disaster happens.
Stop sending new work to a target while allowing existing requests or connections time to finish.
